object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A record of a service outage or problem requiring operational response, created when an alert fires or a customer reports an issue.

source_references.excerpt: Okay. Something breaks. We find out about it, one way or another. Somebody declares an incident, somebody runs it, we fix it, we write it up.
Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence number.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique, never reused? Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification from the monitoring platform or a manually-created record indicating a potential service issue.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, sourced from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket, created when a customer reports an issue to the support system.

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.
And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a support ticket, in a different format than incident numbers.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: IncidentSeverity
object_types.definition: Classification of an incident's technical impact and blast radius, ranging from SEV1 (complete outage) to SEV4 (minor or cosmetic issue).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: IncidentPriority
object_types.definition: Classification of an incident's business urgency, based on customer impact and SLA considerations, ranging from P1 (highest) to P4 (lowest).

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. Which is completely different, and this is the single biggest source of miscommunication in the company. Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: Current operational state of an incident in its lifecycle.

source_references.excerpt: Can an incident be a duplicate of itself? ...That's a strange question. No, obviously not. Then it's worth stating. An incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

inferred_constraints.description: Duplicate relationships must form a directed acyclic graph; no chains allowed. A primary incident should not be a duplicate of any other incident.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. Is a chain wrong, or just untidy? It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A. When we roll up incident counts we only follow one hop, so a chain undercounts.

ambiguities.description: Incident commander is mandatory only for declared incidents, not for triage incidents. The model captures this distinction with a mandatory constraint on the fact type, but the constraint applies conditionally based on incident state. The current formulation may be unclear to implementers about when the constraint applies. Should the constraint be qualified with a state condition, or should there be a separate modeling approach (e.g., objectifying declarations)?

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared. If it turns out to be nothing, it gets closed from triage having never had one. Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: The 'Incident originates from Alert or Ticket' fact type is modeled as ternary with a disjunctive mandatory constraint, but typical usage may be binary (linking incidents to alerts) or binary (linking incidents to tickets) independently. Are these truly three distinct roles (incident, alert-role, ticket-role) all in one relationship, or should they be two separate binary fact types with a combined disjunctive mandatory spanning them?

source_references.excerpt: There's no path to an incident that doesn't have either an alert or a customer report behind it. The form requires you to link at least one.

ambiguities.description: Severity and priority are stated to be independent (lines 65-81), but the model does not capture any exclusion or independence constraint. Should an explicit constraint be added to formalize their independence, or is the independence already implicit from the absence of a linking fact type?

source_references.excerpt: Are they correlated at all? A P1 is always a SEV1. That is not true. It's not true in practice either, and it's the assumption that gets us in trouble. The point stands either way -- they're independent.

ambiguities.description: The transcript mentions that severity can change during an incident (lines 93-97: 'Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius.'). The model captures only the current severity, not historical changes. Should the model include a temporal dimension or an event log for severity changes, or is the 'timeline' mentioned sufficient as a separate concept outside this ORM model?

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident? Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. Is the history of that kept? In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The IncidentState value type lists five states (triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed), but one stakeholder mentions 'monitoring' as something people treat as a state (lines 123-129). The facilitator decided not to model it because it is not in the system dropdown, but this distinction between informal usage and formal state may create confusion. Should a note be added to clarify that 'monitoring' is not a formal state?

source_references.excerpt: There's also 'monitoring,' which sits between mitigated and resolved. That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel. People treat it as a state. People treat lots of things as states. It's not in the dropdown. If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The concept of 'service owner' (the team that owns the service) versus 'incident commander' (the person running this incident) is clarified as distinct, but both are sometimes referred to as 'owner' in casual speech (lines 135-139). The model captures both but does not formally distinguish the two 'owner' roles. The ambiguity is acknowledged in the transcript but left unresolved in the model; clarification in documentation may be needed.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia, you said commander is a role, not a job title. Is there a different sense of owner? There is, and it's the second collision. The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing. Is a service owner a team or a person? And in a channel, 'who owns this?' means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: An incident that is later determined to be caused by customer misconfiguration raises a question about whether it should be reclassified or excluded from reliability metrics. The transcript explicitly parks this decision for later (lines 243-253), and the model does not include any concept of cause classification or incident type. Should the model be extended in the future to capture cause classification when that decision is made, or is it appropriate to keep the model as-is pending a decision from Ravi?

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? No, and it's above all three of us. That's a decision about what we report to the board, and Ravi owns that. Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate relationship has acyclic and irreflexive ring constraints, intended to keep all duplicates pointing directly at a primary incident. However, the facilitator notes this is 'not enforced today' (line 205). Should the model include constraints that reflect what is actually enforced, or what should be enforced? The current choice (to model the intended rule) is documented, but enforcement gap remains a risk.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: The reference modes for Person and Team are inferred as 'person_id' and 'team_id', but the transcript does not explicitly state how persons or teams are identified in the system. Are there existing employee IDs, team codes, or other identifiers? Without explicit confirmation, the choice of reference mode is uncertain and may not match actual system identifiers.
